statement: Square $ABCD$ has side length $4$, with its vertices labeled in order around the square. A point $P$ is chosen at random inside the square. What is the probability that triangle $ABP$ has area greater than $2$ and triangle $BCP$ has area greater than $3$?

choices.misconception: I multiplied the chances that each condition fails, (1/4)(3/8), instead of the chances that each condition holds.
I forgot that the base is 4 and set each height greater than the area itself, so I needed heights above 2 and above 3, giving (1/2)(1/4).
I took away the strip where triangle ABP is too small, 1/4 of the square, and the strip where triangle BCP is too small, 3/8, but forgot to add back the corner where the strips overlap.
I only used the condition on triangle BCP and forgot about triangle ABP.

hints: Each triangle has a side of the square as its base, of length 4. Its area depends only on how far P is from that side.
Triangle ABP has area greater than 2 when P is more than 1 unit from side AB. Triangle BCP has area greater than 3 when P is more than 1.5 units from side BC.
The points that work fill a rectangle 3 by 2.5 inside the 4 by 4 square.

solutions.reliable: Triangle $ABP$ has base $AB = 4$, so its area is $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \cdot h = 2h$, where $h$ is the distance from $P$ to side $AB$. Area greater than $2$ means $h > 1$. In the same way, triangle $BCP$ has area $2k$, where $k$ is the distance from $P$ to side $BC$, and area greater than $3$ means $k > 1.5$. Sides $AB$ and $BC$ are perpendicular, so the points with $h > 1$ and $k > 1.5$ fill a rectangle $3$ by $2.5$, of area $7.5$. The probability is $\frac{7.5}{16} = \frac{15}{32}$.
